source: Fortunato et al. (2018) Science of science (Science review)
finding: Review states teams now author most papers and team size grows about 17 per cent per decade. Small teams disrupt, large teams develop.
numbers: Team-authored share rose from about 50% in 1955 to 90% by 2013 (19.9 M articles, 2.1 M patents). Mean team size grew 17% per decade.
quote: Teams are growing in size, increasing by an average of 17% per decade
limits: A review that cites Wuchty 2007 and Wu 2019. It is not itself a new test. The 17% figure is an average over fields.
agent_relevance: Source of the 17 per cent per decade figure in our SUBFIELDS row. Background only; no direct design rule.

source: Wu, Wang & Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology
finding: Across 65 M papers, patents and software, small teams tend to disrupt and large teams tend to develop existing ideas. Most of the effect is within person, as people move between small and large teams.
numbers: More than 65 million works, 1954-2014. Gap larger for high-impact work. Topic and research design explain only a small part.
quote: smaller teams have tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas and opportunities, whereas larger teams have tended to develop existing ones
limits: Only the abstract and page text were readable (paywall). Disruption is measured by the CD index, which later work showed is sensitive to data artefacts (see b05). Observational.
agent_relevance: Weak support for the idea that team size alone does not set idea novelty. For a scaffold: more agents may help development, not disruption.

source: Lin, Frey & Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas
finding: Remote teams are less likely to produce disruptive work than on-site teams, across fields, periods and team sizes. Remote members share late-stage technical tasks, not conceptual tasks.
numbers: 20,134,803 papers (1960-2020) and 4,060,564 patents (1976-2020). D-score percentile for papers falls from 89 to 84, patents from 76 to 67 (on-site to remote). New concept probability 0.40% to 0.32% (papers); new tech code 3.33% to 3.22% (patents).
limits: Observational. Selection into remote teams is not randomised. Paywalled; abstract and figure captions read.
agent_relevance: Splitting conceptual work across separated agents may lose tacit integration. Keep the framing step in one context.

source: Park, Leahey & Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time
finding: Disruption (CD index) fell across all fields over six decades. Linked to narrower use of past knowledge.
numbers: 45 M papers and 3.9 M patents, six datasets.
limits: Abstract read only. Challenged by Holst et al. (b05) as a dataset artefact. Used here to show that the disruption measure behind the team-size claim is contested.
agent_relevance: Caution: CD-index claims need checking before they guide design.

source: Holst et al. (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: A failed replication of the decline. Entries with zero references create CD=1 outliers that drive the trend. Removing them removes most of the decline.
numbers: 97% of CD5=1 papers (SciSciNet) and 78% of CD5=1 patents (PatentsView) have zero references. In 100 random zero-reference entries, 98% of patents and 93% of papers did have references in the source documents. Monte Carlo with random citing reproduces the decline.
quote: even random citation behavior reproduces the observed decline
limits: Targets Park et al., not Wu et al. directly, but both use the CD family of indices. Full text read.
agent_relevance: Metric hygiene: data artefacts can fake a trend. Check for zero-reference style edge cases in any score we build.

source: Petersen (2015) Quantifying the impact of weak, strong, and super ties in scientific careers (PNAS)
finding: Collaboration networks are mostly weak, short ties. A small set of super ties (extreme-value threshold) coauthor many papers with one person and show an apostle effect: more output and about 17% more citations per paper.
numbers: 473 careers (193 biology, 280 physics), more than 15,000 career years, 94,000 publications, 166,000 collaborators. Top-cited group of 100 per field plus matched Others. Citation boost ratio 1.17 (biology) and 1.16 (physics), about 21 and 8 citations. Super ties often exceed 50% publication overlap.
quote: super ties contribute to above-average productivity and a 17% citation increase per publication
limits: Correlational. Fixed-effects panel regression controls for career age, prestige, team size, prior group experience, but selection (good papers attract partners) is not excluded. Egocentric data only. Two fields.
agent_relevance: Complementary stable pairs help. A fixed pair of agents with distinct roles is a cheap analogue; the human result is not causal.

source: Petersen (2015) super ties: method and caveats
finding: The super-tie label depends on an exponential tail assumption for tie strength. If every tie is a single paper, all ties would be super. Authors say this is rare for large samples.
numbers: Threshold K_c derived analytically per author. Top and Other groups matched on career length and output (at least 52 papers biology, 46 physics).
limits: Sample requires long careers, so survivorship bias is likely. Short or abandoned careers are missing.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise from successful long careers to team design rules.

source: Strong ties in international scientific research collaboration (PMC9844855)
finding: Extension of super ties to country pairs: strong ties raise productivity and citations. Persistent, moderately stable ties give the highest impact.
numbers: 72 countries and regions, 1993-2013. Strong ties are about 1 in 4 collaborators; countries share on average 84% of articles with strong-tie partners.
limits: Unit is the country, not the person. Panel regression, not causal. A supportive extension rather than an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Persistence matters: stable pairings over many tasks beat constant reshuffling, within limits.

source: Scientific success from the perspective of the strength of weak ties (PMC8948253)
finding: Counter-evidence. In DBLP computer science, among scientists with similar achievements, those with weaker ties tend to have the higher h-index, and teams linked by weak ties write more cited papers.
numbers: DBLP coauthorship network, directed asymmetric tie strength. Supports Granovetter weak-tie theory.
limits: Computer science only. No effect sizes extracted in this session. Outcome differs (h-index) from Petersen (per-paper citations).
agent_relevance: Competing view: diverse weak links give novelty, stable strong links give productivity. Both may matter at different stages.

source: Scientific elite revisited: Nobel laureate careers (PMC7211484)
finding: Laureates' careers before the prize look like those of ordinary scientists: hot streaks and rising reliance on collaboration. Impact dips temporarily after the prize.
numbers: Career histories of nearly all Nobel laureates in physics, chemistry and medicine over a century.
limits: Abstract-level numbers only. Survivor sample.
agent_relevance: Elite success is not special team design; do not copy star-team structures.

source: Impactful scientists have higher tendency to involve collaborators in new topics (PNAS, PMC9388131)
finding: Highly productive scientists work with single-topic collaborators; highly cited scientists work with multi-topic collaborators and prefer high-impact partners on new topics.
numbers: Career-level coauthor data across disciplines; compared with controlled surrogate.
limits: Correlational. No effect sizes extracted.
agent_relevance: Breadth of the partner matters for impact, depth for output.

source: Specht & Crowston (2022) Interdisciplinary collaboration from diverse science teams can produce significant outcomes (PLOS ONE)
finding: Team diversity raises paper and citation counts through interdisciplinary process, but lowers member satisfaction and perceived effectiveness. Gender balance offsets this.
numbers: 22 scientific working groups, mixed methods.
limits: Very small number of groups. Trust and leadership mattered qualitatively. Abstract read.
agent_relevance: Diversity costs coordination; a coordinator or verifier role may pay.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Direct LLM test of more team members. Multi-agent systems help on decomposable tasks and hurt on sequential ones. A capability ceiling exists: once the single agent exceeds about 45%, adding agents gives little.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 3 LLM families. Finance Agent: Centralized +80.8% (0.631 vs 0.349), Decentralized +74.5%. Sequential planning: Centralized -50.3%, Decentralized -41.5%, Hybrid -39.1%, Independent -70.0% (vs 0.568). Cross-validated R2 0.373. Right architecture picked for 87% of held-out configs.
quote: architectures without centralized verification tend to propagate errors more
limits: Specific models and benchmarks. Ceiling coefficient -0.236, p=0.004.
agent_relevance: Strong match with the human finding that team benefits are task dependent. Default to a single agent unless the task decomposes.

source: Kim et al. (2025) error amplification in agent teams
finding: Errors spread more in uncoordinated teams than in teams with a central verifier.
numbers: Error amplification factor: Independent 17.2, Decentralized 7.8, Hybrid 5.1, Centralized 4.4. Overhead: Independent 58%, Centralized 285%, Hybrid up to 515%.
limits: Trace-level estimate. Overhead costs are large.
agent_relevance: A verifier role (our guardrails) cuts error spread about fourfold in this test.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest)
finding: Simple sampling and voting over many agents raises accuracy; gains rise with ensemble size and task difficulty. No communication between agents.
numbers: Ensemble size up to 40. Gains: GSM8K +12 to 24 points, MATH +6 to 10, Chess +1 to 4, MMLU +5 to 11, HumanEval +4 to 9. Llama2-13B with 15 agents gets 59% on GSM8K vs Llama2-70B at 54%.
limits: Gains saturate; two code cases where combining with other methods lowered accuracy. Independent samples, so the human analogue is the wisdom of crowds, not teamwork.
agent_relevance: Independence plus voting beats talk for verifiable answers. Cheap to add as a check.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Debate among agents beat a single agent and beat majority voting in the original paper.
numbers: Single agent / Reflection / Majority / Debate: Arithmetic 67.0 / 72.1 / 69.0 / 81.8 %; GSM8K 77.0 / 75.0 / 81.0 / 85.0 %. MMLU persona variant 71.1 to 74.2. 3 agents, 2 rounds.
limits: Later work (b16 to b19) finds the gain often vanishes against strong baselines.
agent_relevance: Original positive result; treat as upper bound.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Debate systems in current form do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling. After hyperparameter tuning some (Multi-Persona) do better, so they are fragile.
numbers: Multiple-choice benchmarks with cost and time trade-offs. Exact scores not extracted.
quote: multi-agent debating systems, in their current form, do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies
limits: Only abstract and first page read.
agent_relevance: Debate is sensitive to settings, so a gain is not safe to assume.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt matches the best discussion method. Discussion beats single agent only when the prompt has no demonstrations.
numbers: Tasks include ECQA, GSM8K and FOLIO-wiki with ChatGPT-3.5 and other backbones. Exact margins not extracted.
limits: Mainly older models.
agent_relevance: The gain from team talk may just be a better prompt. Test against a strong single-agent prompt first.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five debate methods on nine benchmarks and four models often fail to beat Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, even with more compute. Mixing different models helps.
numbers: Heter-MAD: about +6.4% average over SoM average and +5.8% vs CoT average for one variant; other variants +2.1 to +4.4% vs CoT average.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines
limits: Gains vary by benchmark, some negative (for example MBPP -10.8% in one row).
agent_relevance: Different model families act like diverse team members. Same-model teams add little.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial?
finding: Mixing different models lowers average quality. Repeatedly sampling the best model (Self-MoA) beats mixing in most settings. Quality matters more than diversity.
numbers: Self-MoA beats Mixed-MoA by 6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 and by 3.8% on average across MMLU, CRUX, MATH. Over 200 experiments on the quality-diversity trade-off.
limits: Partly conflicts with b18: mixing helps when members are close in strength and hurts when one is much weaker.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: diversity helps only if members are close in strength.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Failures of agent teams fall in 14 modes in three groups: specification and design, inter-agent misalignment, verification.
numbers: 1,600+ annotated traces, 7 frameworks, 150 traces used to build the taxonomy, kappa 0.88. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across frameworks. A prompt and role fix alone gave +9.4% success for ChatDev. Modes: reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, no completion awareness 12.4%.
limits: Open-source frameworks and older models at time of study.
agent_relevance: Matches human team failures (role confusion, no clarifying questions). Role specs and verification are the cheap fixes.

source: Qian et al. (2025) Scaling LLM-based multi-agent collaboration (MacNet)
finding: Performance grows with number of agents along a logistic curve, with emergence earlier than in neural scaling. Irregular topologies beat regular ones.
numbers: Up to 1,000+ agents (2^6 nodes mesh). Quality: CoT 0.5757, AgentVerse 0.5805, MacNet-Random 0.6522, Mesh 0.6316, Chain 0.6078. About 2^4 nodes judged a reasonable size.
limits: Four tasks, one model; win varies by task (Chain MMLU 0.6632 but HumanEval 0.3720). Cost grows with node count.
agent_relevance: Moderate team size with sparse links is enough; no need for hundreds of agents.

source: Chen et al. (2024) AgentVerse: facilitating multi-agent collaboration and exploring emergent behaviors
finding: Team of LLM agents shows social behaviour: volunteering, conformity and destructive acts. Weaker agents are swayed by wrong feedback.
numbers: About 10% of errors on MGSM trace to a correct agent being talked out of its answer by another (GPT-3.5 agents). Not seen with GPT-4 agents.
limits: Partial read.
agent_relevance: Conformity is a known group risk; guard with independent first answers.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: A multi-agent generate, debate, rank loop improves hypothesis quality with more test-time compute, with no saturation seen. Experts preferred it on novelty and impact.
numbers: 203 research goals; Elo of top hypotheses rose across ten time buckets. Surpassed other frontier LLMs in Elo. AML repurposing candidates tested in vitro.
limits: Elo is self-rated by the system, not independent. Expert evaluation on small sets. Partial read.
agent_relevance: Tournament ranking inside one loop is a team-style mechanism worth a cheap test.

source: Swanson et al. (2025) The Virtual Lab of AI agents designs new SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies
finding: An LLM PI agent leads LLM scientist agents with human feedback. It designed 92 nanobodies; two showed better binding to JN.1 or KP.3 variants.
numbers: 92 designs, experimental ELISA validation. Pipeline used ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, Rosetta.
limits: Abstract only (paywall). No single-agent control in the abstract. Human guidance in loop.
agent_relevance: Existence proof, not a test that team structure caused the success.

source: Wuchty, Jones & Uzzi (2007) The increasing dominance of teams in production of knowledge
finding: Founding study of team growth and higher citation of team papers. Not opened (blocked by challenge page). Figures reported only via b01.
numbers: See b01.
limits: Not read in this session.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Gap note: replication status of Wu 2019
finding: No independent replication of Wu 2019 found in this session. Nearest test, Lin 2023, agrees in direction for remote vs on-site, and Holst 2024 refutes the related Park 2023 trend.
numbers: Lin 2023: new-concept probability 0.40% to 0.32%.
limits: Absence of evidence only. Search budget was exhausted; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Treat the small-team disruption effect as single-source.
